claim: Different subtypes of interneurons destined for the olfactory bulb are continuously generated by neural stem cells located in the ventricular and subventricular zones along the lateral forebrain ventricles of mice.
source: Different subtypes of interneurons, destined for the olfactory bulb, are continuously generated by neural stem cells located in the ventricular and subventricular zones along the lateral forebrain ventricles of mice.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field of adult neurogenesis, supported by extensive prior research.

claim: Neuronal identity in the olfactory bulb depends on the existence of defined microdomains of pre-determined neural stem cells along the ventricle walls.
source: Neuronal identity in the olfactory bulb depends on the existence of defined microdomains of pre-determined neural stem cells along the ventricle walls.
evidence: This statement is supported by references to lineage studies in the manuscript.

claim: The transcription factor Vax1 controls the production of two specific neuronal subtypes in the olfactory bulb.
source: Here, we show that the transcription factor Vax1 controls the production of two specific neuronal subtypes.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Vax1 is directly necessary to generate Calbindin expressing interneurons from ventro-lateral progenitors.
source: First, it is directly necessary to generate Calbindin expressing interneurons from ventro-lateral progenitors.
evidence: This is supported by conditional knockout experiments showing loss of CB-N when Vax1 is deleted.

claim: Vax1 represses the generation of dopaminergic neurons by dorsolateral progenitors through inhibition of Pax6 expression.
source: Second, it represses the generation of dopaminergic neurons by dorsolateral progenitors through inhibition of Pax6 expression.
evidence: This is supported by overexpression experiments showing reduced Pax6 and DA-N when Vax1 is overexpressed.

claim: Vax1 repression of Pax6 occurs, at least in part, via activation of microRNA miR-7.
source: We present data indicating that this repression occurs, at least in part, via activation of microRNA miR-7.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data showing increased miR-7 levels upon Vax1 overexpression and bioinformatic identification of Vax1 binding sites in miR-7 promoters.

claim: New interneuron precursors are continuously generated by neural stem cell populations along the walls of the lateral ventricles in the postnatal and adult rodent forebrain.
source: In the postnatal and adult rodent forebrain, new interneuron precursors are continuously generated by neural stem cell populations along the walls of the lateral ventricles.
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature in the field.

claim: After amplification in the subventricular zone and long-distance migration via the rostral migratory stream, interneuron precursors are added to the preexisting circuitry of the olfactory bulb.
source: After their amplification in the subventricular zone (SVZ) and long-distance migration via the rostral migratory stream (RMS) they are added to the preexisting circuitry of the olfactory bulb (OB) (Alvarez-Buylla and Garcia-Verdugo, 2002; Whitman and Greer, 2009; Platel et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: OB interneurons produced in the SVZ-RMS-OB neurogenic system show a wide spectrum of phenotypic diversity at the levels of morphology, terminal position, connectivity, and neurotransmitter use.
source: OB interneurons produced in this SVZ-RMS-OB neurogenic system show a wide spectrum of phenotypic diversity at the levels of morphology, terminal position, connectivity, and neurotransmitter use (Whitman and Greer, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: The diversity of OB interneurons relies on the existence of defined microdomains of predetermined neural stem cells in the ventricular-subventricular zone.
source: Lineage studies demonstrated that this diversity relies on the existence of defined microdomains of predetermined neural stem cells in the ventricular-subventricular zone [V-SVZ (Merkle et al., 2007; Ventura and Goldman, 2007; Lledo et al., 2008; Fiorelli et al., 2015; Chaker et al., 2016)].
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to lineage tracing studies.

claim: Gli1 activation by Sonic Hedgehog is necessary to generate Calbindin-expressing periglomerular neurons in the ventral aspect of the ventricular wall.
source: It has been shown that Gli1 activation by Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) is necessary to generate Calbindin-expressing periglomerular neurons (CB-N) in the ventral aspect of the ventricular wall (Ihrie et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The zinc-finger transcription factors Zic1 and Zic2 act as inducers of Calretinin-expressing GABAergic interneurons in the dorso-septal region.
source: Moreover, the zinc-finger transcription factors (TF) Zic1 and Zic2 act as inducers of Calretinin (CR)-expressing GABAergic interneurons in the dorso-septal region (Tiveron et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Dopaminergic OB interneurons are generated by neural stem cells located in the dorsal and dorso-lateral aspects of the ventricular wall.
source: This is exemplified by the regulation of a group of OB interneurons that, in addition to GABA, use dopamine as their main neurotransmitter (DA-N). This neuron type is generated by neural stem cells located in the dorsal and dorso-lateral aspects of the ventricular wall.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: Pax6 is a key determinant of dopaminergic neuron cell type in the olfactory bulb.
source: Pax6 is a key determinant of this cell type (Hack et al., 2005; Kohwi et al., 2005) and is expressed in the entire lineage from stem cells to neurons (Hack et al., 2005; de Chevigny et al., 2012b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Pax6 is expressed in the entire lineage from stem cells to neurons in the dopaminergic neuron lineage.
source: Pax6 is a key determinant of this cell type (Hack et al., 2005; Kohwi et al., 2005) and is expressed in the entire lineage from stem cells to neurons (Hack et al., 2005; de Chevigny et al., 2012b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Pax6 mRNA expression in the postnatal ventricular wall is not restricted to the DA-N producing dorsal progenitor pool, but extends far into the lateral region.
source: Indeed, Pax6 mRNA expression in the postnatal ventricular wall is not restricted to the DA-N producing dorsal progenitor pool, but extends far into the lateral region where other cell types, including purely GABAergic granule cells and CB-N, are produced.
evidence: This is supported by prior research cited in the manuscript.

claim: The microRNA miR-7 is present in a Pax6-opposing ventro-dorsal gradient and precludes Pax6 mRNA translation, restricting protein expression and DA-N phenotype to the dorsal region.
source: However, the presence of the microRNA miR-7 in a Pax6-opposing ventro-dorsal gradient precludes Pax6 mRNA translation and restricts protein expression, and consequently DA-N phenotype, to the dorsal region (de Chevigny et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Vax1 is an intracellular mediator of SHH signaling.
source: The Ventral Homeodomain Protein 1 (Vax1), an intracellular mediator of SHH signaling, is expressed in ventral territories of the developing mouse forebrain as well as in ventral aspects of the developing eye (Hallonet et al., 1999; Ohsaki et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Vax1 is expressed in ventral territories of the developing mouse forebrain and in ventral aspects of the developing eye.
source: The Ventral Homeodomain Protein 1 (Vax1), an intracellular mediator of SHH signaling, is expressed in ventral territories of the developing mouse forebrain as well as in ventral aspects of the developing eye (Hallonet et al., 1999; Ohsaki et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The expression pattern of Vax1 is complementary to that of Pax6 in both the developing forebrain and eye.
source: In both systems, the expression pattern of Vax1 is complementary to that of Pax6, and genetic studies provided evidence for cross regulatory interactions between both factors (Hallonet et al., 1998; Bertuzzi et al., 1999; Hallonet et al., 1999; Stoykova et al., 2000; Bäumer et al., 2002; Mui et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Genetic studies provide evidence for cross regulatory interactions between Vax1 and Pax6.
source: In both systems, the expression pattern of Vax1 is complementary to that of Pax6, and genetic studies provided evidence for cross regulatory interactions between both factors (Hallonet et al., 1998; Bertuzzi et al., 1999; Hallonet et al., 1999; Stoykova et al., 2000; Bäumer et al., 2002; Mui et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Constitutive Vax1 mutants show a strong decrease in GABAergic interneurons in the developing neocortex at embryonic stages.
source: At embryonic stages, constitutive Vax1 mutants show a strong decrease in GABAergic interneurons in the developing neocortex, indicating an essential function in their generation (Taglialatela et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Vax1 homozygous mutants generally die at perinatal stages and only few 'escapers' survive for a few weeks after birth.
source: Vax-1 homozygous mutants die generally at perinatal stages and only few 'escapers' survive for a few weeks after birth.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In Vax1 homozygous mutant 'escapers', the entire postnatal SVZ-RMS-OB neurogenic system is severely compromised, showing accumulation of precursors in the SVZ and severe disorganization of the RMS.
source: In these animals, the entire postnatal SVZ-RMS-OB neurogenic system is severely compromised, showing accumulation of precursors in the SVZ and severe disorganization of the RMS (Soria et al., 2004), altogether precluding a detailed analysis of Vax1-function at later stages.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Vax1 mRNA is present in a ventro-dorsal gradient along the lateral wall of the forebrain ventricles based on high-resolution gene expression screening.
source: Indeed, based on a high-resolution gene expression screen, comparing the postnatal pallial and subpallial OB lineages, we found that Vax1 mRNA is present in a ventro-dorsal gradient along the lateral wall of the forebrain ventricles.
evidence: This is supported by microarray data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Vax1 is essential for the generation of CB-N by the ventral stem cell pool.
source: Functional studies using conditional mutants demonstrate that Vax1 is essential for the generation of CB-N by the ventral stem cell pool.
evidence: This is supported by conditional knockout experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Vax1 acts as negative regulator of DA-N OB fate via downregulation of the pro-dopaminergic factor Pax6.
source: Moreover, we show that Vax1 acts as negative regulator of DA-N OB fate via downregulation of the pro-dopaminergic factor Pax6.
evidence: This is supported by overexpression experiments showing reduced Pax6 and DA-N.

claim: Vax1 repressor function is, at least in part, mediated by induction of miR-7.
source: Finally, we provide data suggesting that this repressor function is, at least in part, mediated by induction of miR-7.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data and bioinformatic analysis.

claim: Vax1 mRNA was confined to the neurogenic lineage derived from the lateral ventricular wall based on microarray analyses.
source: These analyses showed that Vax1 was confined to the neurogenic lineage derived from the lateral ventricular wall (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Vax1 expression strongly increased at 2dpe and remained stably high at 4dpe when most cells were migratory neuronal precursors.
source: Expression strongly increased at 2dpe and remained stably high at 4dpe, when most cells were migratory neuronal precursors, before steeply decreasing at 7dpe when cells arrived in the OB and emigrated from the RMS to invade the granule cell (GCL) and the glomerular (GL) layers (Tiveron et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data and citation to prior characterization.

claim: Vax1 expression steeply decreased at 7dpe when cells arrived in the OB and emigrated from the RMS to invade the granule cell and glomerular layers.
source: Expression strongly increased at 2dpe and remained stably high at 4dpe, when most cells were migratory neuronal precursors, before steeply decreasing at 7dpe when cells arrived in the OB and emigrated from the RMS to invade the granule cell (GCL) and the glomerular (GL) layers (Tiveron et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data and citation to prior characterization.

claim: Isolates from dorsally electroporated brains showed no obvious Vax1 mRNA expression over all analyzed time points.
source: In comparison, isolates from dorsally electroporated brains showed no obvious Vax1 mRNA expression over all analyzed time points (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Vax1 mRNA always showed a gradient-like distribution along the lateral ventricular wall, with highest expression in the ventral-most aspect and extending far into dorsal regions.
source: Vax1 mRNA always showed a gradient-like distribution along the lateral ventricular wall, with highest expression in the ventral-most aspect and extending far into dorsal regions (Figure 1C,D,E,F).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization images shown in Figures 1C-F.

claim: Fainter Vax1 expression was observed along the septal wall.
source: Fainter expression was observed along the septal wall.
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization observations.

claim: Vax1 mRNA was excluded from the VZ but expressed in the underlying SVZ in the lateral wall.
source: In the lateral wall, Vax1 mRNA was excluded from the VZ but expressed in the underlying SVZ (Figure 1C',D',E',F').
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization images shown in Figures 1C'-F'.

claim: Vax1 mRNA in the lateral wall was generally non-overlapping with PAX6.
source: Vax1 mRNA in the lateral wall was generally non-overlapping with PAX6, a marker for the dorsal stem cell pool and a determinant for the DA-N lineage (Figure C,C').
evidence: This is supported by combined in situ hybridization and immunohistochemistry shown in Figures 1C and C'.

claim: 3.3%±0.32 of Vax1 mRNA-positive cells expressed ASCL1, a marker for transit amplifying precursors.
source: Vax1 mRNA-positive cells rarely expressed ASCL1 (3.3%±0.32), a marker for transit amplifying precursors (Figure 1D,D'), but the vast majority was labeled with a DLX2 antibody (90%±0.89) (Figure 1E,E'; arrowheads), confirming the preferential expression of Vax1 in migratory neuronal precursors (Doetsch et al., 2002; Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of double-labeled cells from in situ hybridization and immunohistochemistry.

claim: 90%±0.89 of Vax1 mRNA-positive cells were labeled with a DLX2 antibody, confirming the preferential expression of Vax1 in migratory neuronal precursors.
source: Vax1 mRNA-positive cells rarely expressed ASCL1 (3.3%±0.32), a marker for transit amplifying precursors (Figure 1D,D'), but the vast majority was labeled with a DLX2 antibody (90%±0.89) (Figure 1E,E'; arrowheads), confirming the preferential expression of Vax1 in migratory neuronal precursors (Doetsch et al., 2002; Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of double-labeled cells and citation to prior characterization of DLX2 as a neuroblast marker.

claim: About one third (32.6%±3.07) of the Vax1+ cells in the SVZ expressed the proliferation marker KI67, likely representing mitotic neuroblasts.
source: Finally, about one third (32.6%±3.07) of the Vax1+ cells in the SVZ expressed the proliferation marker KI67 (Figure 1F,F', arrowheads), likely representing mitotic neuroblasts.
evidence: This is supported by quantification of double-labeled cells from in situ hybridization and immunohistochemistry.

claim: In the RMS, Vax1 mRNA was present in a ventro-dorsal gradient, complementary to PAX6 immunostaining.
source: In the RMS, Vax1 mRNA was also present in a ventro-dorsal gradient, complementary to PAX6 immunostaining (Figure 1G), although this organization was less evident than in the SVZ, probably due to cell intermingling in this migratory compartment (Figure 1G', G").
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization and immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Vax1 mRNA in the RMS co-localized strongly with DLX2 immunoreactivity.
source: Like in the SVZ, Vax1 mRNA in the RMS co-localized strongly with DLX2 immunoreactivity (Figure 1H, close up H', H').
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization and immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Vax1 is expressed in the lateral and ventral SVZ in a subset of proliferating precursors and in most neuroblasts, the latter maintaining expression during their migration in the RMS.
source: Altogether, the combination of microarray studies in defined neuronal lineages and histological approaches led to the conclusion that Vax1 is expressed in the lateral and ventral SVZ in a subset of proliferating precursors and in most neuroblasts, the latter maintaining expression during their migration in the RMS.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple experimental approaches presented in the manuscript.

claim: Vax1 has been shown to act as an intracellular mediator of SHH signaling.
source: As Vax1 is strongly expressed in this area, and has been shown to act as an intracellular mediator of SHH signaling (Take-uchi et al., 2003; Furimsky and Wallace, 2006; Zhao et al., 2010), we first asked if the TF is implicated in the generation of the CB-N subtype.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Quantification of labeled neurons in the GCL and GL revealed no significant differences between control and Vax1 mutant mice.
source: Quantification of labeled neurons in the GCL and GL revealed no significant differences between control and mutant mice (Figure 2C; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: TH-positive PGC were not significantly affected in Vax1 conditional mutants.
source: TH-positive PGC were also not significantly affected (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: There was a significant loss in the small population of CB-positive neurons in the GL in Vax1 conditional mutants.
source: However, there was a significant loss in the small population of CB-positive neurons in the GL (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Vax1 expression in the ventro-lateral-derived neurogenic lineage is necessary for the correct generation of CB-N in the GL.
source: Thus, Vax1 expression in the ventro-lateral-derived neurogenic lineage is necessary for the correct generation of CB-N in the GL.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the conditional knockout data showing loss of CB-N.

claim: Vax1 mRNA showed a steep ventro-dorsal gradient in micro-dissected V-SVZ tissue, opposed to and partially overlapping with Pax6 mRNA localization.
source: In agreement with the histological data, Vax1 mRNA showed a steep ventro-dorsal gradient, opposed to, and partially overlapping with, the well-described localization of Pax6 mRNA, that extends dorso-ventrally (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1; de Chevigny et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Several studies provided evidence that Vax1 can negatively regulate Pax6 expression during development.
source: First, several studies provided evidence that Vax1 can negatively regulate Pax6 expression during development (Bertuzzi et al., 1999; Hallonet et al., 1999; Mui et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Repression of Pax6 translation along the lateral wall is necessary to confine Pax6 protein, and consequently DA-N phenotype, to the dorsal stem cell pool.
source: Second, repression of Pax6 translation along the lateral wall is necessary to confine Pax6 protein, and consequently DA-N phenotype, to the dorsal stem cell pool (de Chevigny et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: GFP-positive cells generated in both dorsal and lateral compartments showed a significant decrease in Pax6 expression levels two days after Vax1 overexpression.
source: Two days later, animals were sacrificed and intensity of Pax6 immunostaining in GFP-positive cells was measured in the dorsal and dorso-lateral SVZ (Figure 3C,D,E). GFP-positive cells generated in both compartments showed a significant decrease in Pax6 expression levels at this early time point (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of immunofluorescence intensity shown in Figure 3E.

claim: 15 and 25 days after pCAG-Vax1 electroporation into the dorsal wall, the proportion of GFP-positive neurons that showed Pax6 expression was reduced by over 80%.
source: Then we asked if Pax6 expression was affected at late time points, after the arrival of newborn neurons in the OB GL. Indeed, 15 and 25 days after pCAG-Vax1 electroporation into the dorsal wall the proportion of GFP-positive neurons that showed Pax6 expression was reduced by over 80% (Figure 3F,G).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Vax1 has the capacity to act as a negative regulator of Pax6 expression during postnatal OB neurogenesis.
source: We conclude that Vax1 has the capacity to act as a negative regulator of Pax6 expression during postnatal OB neurogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the overexpression experiments showing reduced Pax6.

claim: DA-N in the OB GL are derived from the dorsal and dorso-lateral aspects of the ventricle walls.
source: DA-N in the OB GL are derived from the dorsal and dorso-lateral aspects of the ventricle walls (Merkle et al., 2007; Fernández et al., 2011; de Chevigny et al., 2012a) and Pax6 expression is necessary and sufficient for the acquisition of this neurotransmitter phenotype (Hack et al., 2005; Kohwi et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Pax6 expression is necessary and sufficient for the acquisition of dopaminergic neurotransmitter phenotype.
source: DA-N in the OB GL are derived from the dorsal and dorso-lateral aspects of the ventricle walls (Merkle et al., 2007; Fernández et al., 2011; de Chevigny et al., 2012a) and Pax6 expression is necessary and sufficient for the acquisition of this neurotransmitter phenotype (Hack et al., 2005; Kohwi et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Ectopic expression of Vax1 in the dorsal compartment led to a significant loss of TH/GFP-positive neurons 15 days later in the OB.
source: Ectopic expression of Vax1 led to a significant loss of TH/GFP-positive neurons 15 days later in the OB (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Loss of TH-positive cells after Vax1 overexpression was robust over time and could be observed at 25 and 60 dpe.
source: Loss of TH-positive cells was robust over time and could be observed at 25 and 60 dpe (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The number of CR-N of the glomerular layer was unaffected by Vax1 expression.
source: First, the number of the second major identified neuron type that is generated in the dorsal ventricular wall, CR-N of the glomerular layer (Fernández et al., 2011; Tiveron et al., 2017), was unaffected by Vax1 expression (Figure 4B), arguing against a fate shift toward this neuron type (Tiveron et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The density of total GFP+ cells in the GL of Vax1-electroporated animals was significantly reduced.
source: Second, the density of total GFP+ cells in the GL of Vax1-electroporated animals was significantly reduced (Figure 4D), whereas the number of GFP+ granule cells was not affected (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The number of GFP+ granule cells was not affected by Vax1 overexpression in the dorsal compartment.
source: Second, the density of total GFP+ cells in the GL of Vax1-electroporated animals was significantly reduced (Figure 4D), whereas the number of GFP+ granule cells was not affected (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Overexpression of Vax1 in the lateral wall induced a significant loss of TH-positive neurons in the GL 15 days later.
source: Overexpression of Vax1 in the lateral wall induced a significant loss of TH-positive neurons in the GL 15 days later (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Numbers of CB-N and CR-N were unchanged 15 days after Vax1 overexpression in the lateral wall.
source: At the same time point, numbers of CB-N and CR-N were unchanged (Figure 4F), indicating again that no phenotypic switch toward these subtypes occurred.
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The density of GFP+ cells was unaffected in both GL and GCL after Vax1 overexpression in the lateral wall.
source: The density of GFP+ cells was also unaffected in both GL (Figure 4G) and GCL (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Vax1 overexpression specifically inhibits DA-N phenotype of newborn neurons in the OB.
source: Thus, Vax1 overexpression specifically inhibits DA-N phenotype of newborn neurons in the OB.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the overexpression experiments showing selective loss of DA-N.

claim: Vax1 loss-of-function analyses failed to show a significant increase in DA-N at a confidence level of p≤0.05.
source: These analyses failed to show a significant increase in DA-N at a confidence level of p≤0.05 (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Vax1, likely via regulation of Pax6, has the capacity to negatively control the generation of DA-N for the OB.
source: We conclude that Vax1, likely via regulation of Pax6, has the capacity to negatively control the generation of DA-N for the OB.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined data showing Vax1 represses Pax6 and DA-N generation.

claim: While Vax1 is necessary for the generation of CB-N, it is not sufficient.
source: Moreover, these data show that while Vax1 is necessary for the generation of CB-N, it is not sufficient.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Vax1 overexpression does not increase CB-N numbers.

claim: Mature microRNA miR-7 is expressed in a ventro-dorsal gradient along the lateral ventricular wall and post-transcriptionally inhibits Pax6 protein expression.
source: Previous work demonstrated that mature microRNA miR-7 is expressed in a ventro-dorsal gradient along the lateral ventricular wall and post-transcriptionally inhibits Pax6 protein expression.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The interaction between miR-7 and Pax6 confines the generation of DA-N to the very dorso-lateral aspect.
source: This interaction confines the generation of DA-N to the very dorso-lateral aspect (de Chevigny et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Augmented Vax1 expression led to a strong increase in miR-7 levels.
source: qRT-PCR analyses demonstrated that augmented Vax1 expression (Figure 5B) led to a strong increase in miR-7 levels (Figure 5C), suggesting that Vax1 regulates MiR-7 expression.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Bioinformatical analyses identified a significant match of the Vax1 DNA binding motif within 500 bp of the transcription start site of each of the three MiR-7 loci present in the mouse genome.
source: In agreement, bioinformatical analyses of the proximal promoters of the three MiR-7 loci (MiR-7–1, MiR-7–2, MiR-7b) identified a significant match of the Vax1 DNA binding motif within 500 bp of the transcription start site of each of the three MiR-7 loci present in the mouse genome (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The negative impact of Vax1 on Pax6 expression is, at least in part, mediated via the positive regulation of MiR-7.
source: Altogether, these results suggest that the negative impact of Vax1 on Pax6 expression is, at least in part, mediated via the positive regulation of MiR-7.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined data showing Vax1 increases miR-7 and has Vax1 binding sites in miR-7 promoters.

claim: Vax1 is strongly expressed in the ventral stem cell compartment of the OB neurogenic system where it is necessary for the generation of CB-N.
source: Here, we show that Vax1 is strongly expressed in the ventral stem cell compartment of the OB neurogenic system where it is necessary for the generation of CB-N.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: Vax1 acts as a negative regulator of Pax6, likely via the induction of miR-7, thereby restricting the generation of DA-N.
source: In addition to this actively phenotype-determining function, our data show that Vax1 acts as a negative regulator of Pax6, likely via the induction of miR-7, thereby restricting the generation of DA-N, which are generated in a neighboring progenitor domain (Figure 5E; de Chevigny et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: During nervous system development, determination of neuronal phenotype is controlled by the combinatorial expression of transcription factors.
source: During nervous system development, determination of neuronal phenotype is controlled by the combinatorial expression of transcription factors (Flames et al., 2007; Guillemot, 2007; Lai et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Cross regulatory interactions between transcription factors have been shown to tightly define progenitor domains that generate specific neuron subtypes.
source: Moreover, cross regulatory interactions between such TFs have been shown to tightly define progenitor domains that generate specific neuron subtypes (Jessell, 2000; Sagner and Briscoe, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Regionalization of the postnatal stem cell compartment has been shown to depend on spatially restricted and combinatorial expression of TFs like Pax6, Emx1, Gsx1/2, Gli1/2, or Zic1/2.
source: In agreement, regionalization of the postnatal stem cell compartment has been shown to depend on spatially restricted and combinatorial expression of TFs like, for example, Pax6, Emx1, Gsx1/2, Gli1/2, or Zic1/2 (Alvarez-Buylla et al., 2008; Weinandy et al., 2011; Fiorelli et al., 2015; Angelova et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: CB-N are produced by NSCs positioned in the ventral aspect of the V-SVZ.
source: CB-N are produced by NSCs positioned in the ventral aspect of the V-SVZ (Merkle et al., 2007) and SHH signaling, via its effector GLI1, has been implicated in the specification of this subtype (Ihrie et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: SHH signaling, via its effector GLI1, has been implicated in the specification of CB-N.
source: CB-N are produced by NSCs positioned in the ventral aspect of the V-SVZ (Merkle et al., 2007) and SHH signaling, via its effector GLI1, has been implicated in the specification of this subtype (Ihrie et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Previous work demonstrated that Vax1 expression is positively controlled by SHH signaling.
source: Interestingly, previous work demonstrated that Vax1 expression is positively controlled by SHH signaling (Hallonet et al., 1999; Take-uchi et al., 2003; Furimsky and Wallace, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: It appears probable that Vax1 acts downstream of SHH expression in the ventral SVZ to control CB-N production for the OB.
source: In light of our finding that Vax1 deletion also leads to specific loss of CB-N, it appears probable that Vax1 acts downstream of SHH expression in the ventral SVZ to control CB-N production for the OB.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data on SHH, Vax1, and CB-N.

claim: Forced expression of Vax1 in the Pax6-positive domains was sufficient to reduce PAX6 protein expression and to inhibit the production of DA-N, but not of other neuron types, in the OB.
source: Forced expression of Vax1 in the Pax6-positive domains was sufficient to reduce PAX6 protein expression and to inhibit the production of DA-N, but not of other neuron types, in the OB.
evidence: This is supported by the overexpression experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: The ventro-dorsally oriented Vax1 gradient as well as the graded expression of Pax6 and miR-7 are maintained in adult stages.
